region: Indo-West Pacific — India & Southeast Asia to Japan
description: A smooth-skinned seahorse of estuaries, seagrass beds and mangrove edges that anchors itself to weed with its prehensile tail. The male carries the eggs in a sealed brood pouch and releases several hundred fry about 7 mm long after two to three weeks.

region: Western Atlantic — Nova Scotia to Venezuela, incl. Gulf of Mexico
description: Named for the fine pale lines that trace its neck and head, it clings to seagrass, sponges, gorgonians and drifting Sargassum. Captive-bred stock takes frozen mysis readily and is among the hardiest seahorses kept.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil
description: A slender, long-snouted seahorse of Caribbean reefs and seagrass that often turns vivid yellow, orange or red sprinkled with white freckles. Males release very small fry, sometimes more than a thousand at a time, which spend weeks drifting in the plankton.

region: Southern Australia, Tasmania & New Zealand
description: The largest seahorse in the hobby, living among kelp, sponges and jetty piles in cool southern waters; adult males carry a huge, pale brood pouch. Newborns are unusually large (around 1.5 cm) and take newly hatched brine shrimp from birth.

region: Gulf of Mexico, Florida, Bahamas & Bermuda
description: One of the smallest fishes in the hobby, rarely exceeding 2.5 cm, living among Zostera and other seagrasses in shallow bays. It needs live baby brine shrimp and breeds continuously in small dedicated tanks, males releasing small broods every couple of weeks.

region: Philippines, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: A spiny seahorse of shallow seagrass and algae flats near reefs, usually pale cream to yellow with reddish-brown lines on the snout and body. Captive-bred specimens are increasingly available.

region: Southeast Asia — Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia & Indonesia
description: Named for the alternating yellow and black rings on its tail, this spiny seahorse lives on coral reefs among sponges and soft corals. Males brood for about two weeks before releasing fry that drift in the plankton.

region: Eastern Australia — New South Wales & southern Queensland
description: Endemic to sheltered bays and estuaries of eastern Australia, where it clings to sponges, soft corals and even protective swimming-enclosure nets. Listed as Endangered, it is bred in Sydney public aquaria for release back into the wild.

region: Eastern Pacific — southern California to Peru & the Galápagos
description: The largest seahorse of the Americas, living among kelp, gorgonians and rocky reefs from California to Peru. Usually reddish-brown to gold with fine pale lines, it is a familiar species in public aquaria.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Japan & Hawaii
description: Covered in long, sharp, often dark-tipped spines and with a very long snout, it lives on sand and rubble slopes among sponges and algae, often deeper than other seahorses. It is usually found singly.

region: Eastern Atlantic — Senegal to Angola
description: The only seahorse along much of tropical West Africa, found in seagrass, algae beds and estuaries from Senegal to Angola. A large, robust species with a modest coronet, seen mainly in public aquaria.

region: Northeast Atlantic & Mediterranean
description: A short-snouted, smooth-bodied European seahorse found over sand, mud and seagrass from the British Isles to the Mediterranean. It often sits in open areas rather than dense weed, and is bred in several European public aquaria.

region: Northeast Atlantic & Mediterranean
description: Recognised by fleshy filaments forming a 'mane' along its neck and back and a scatter of tiny white dots, it lives in seagrass and algae beds from the British Isles to the Mediterranean. Newborns are relatively large and settle quickly among weed.

region: Indo-West Pacific — India to Japan & northern Australia
description: Identified by three small dark spots along the top of the trunk and a sharp, hooked spine above each eye. It lives on sand and rubble, often deeper than other seahorses, and is heavily traded for traditional medicine.

region: Southern Australia
description: A small, knobbly seahorse of southern Australian algae beds, often covered in short skin filaments and marked with dark-ringed white spots. It is frequently found in small groups and is bred in Australian public aquaria.

region: South Africa — Knysna, Swartvlei & Keurbooms estuaries
description: Confined to a handful of estuaries on South Africa's southern coast, it lives among eelgrass and algae in water whose salinity swings with tide and rainfall. Endangered, it is bred in several aquaria as an insurance population.

region: Indo-West Pacific — India to the Philippines & northern Australia
description: A very spiny seahorse with long, sharp body spines, living on deeper sand and rubble bottoms among sponges. It is one of the species most often caught as trawl bycatch in Southeast Asia.

region: Indo-Pacific — eastern Indian Ocean to Samoa, north to Japan
description: Lives in pairs in caves and under ledges on coral reefs, often swimming upside-down along the ceiling. Banded red and white with a red-and-white fan tail, it picks parasites off other fishes, and the male carries the eggs glued to a brood area under the trunk.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to New Caledonia
description: Shaped like the ringed pipefish but banded dark red on yellow, it lives in caves and under ledges on deeper reef slopes. Pairs court side by side before the female transfers her eggs to the male.

region: Indian Ocean & Red Sea to Indonesia
description: Told apart from its relatives by broad red bands separated by narrow pale rings. Usually seen in pairs in caves and crevices on reef slopes, with a red fan tail edged in white.

region: Red Sea & Indian Ocean to the Andaman Sea
description: Has many more and narrower red rings than its relatives, and a red tail with a white margin. It hovers in caves and under overhangs on Red Sea and Indian Ocean reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to the Gulf of California
description: A tiny cave-dwelling pipefish, orange-red with an electric-blue stripe from snout to tail, found in pairs under ledges. It feeds on copepods, will clean other fishes, and breeds in mature reef tanks.

region: Western Pacific — Thailand & the Philippines to the Solomon Islands & northern Australia
description: Orange in the middle of the body with a dark bluish head and tail, it runs 'cleaning stations' in reef caves where it picks parasites off visiting fishes. Pairs stay together, and the male broods the eggs on his belly.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines to Australia & Samoa
description: A bottom-living pipefish that glides over sand, rubble and live rock picking off copepods, its pale body covered in a dark scribbled network. It needs a mature reef with a large population of tiny crustaceans.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: Common on shallow reef flats and lagoons, it rests on sand and rubble between corals, marked with paired dark bands and fine red lines on the head. The male carries the eggs in an open brood area on the underside of the trunk.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the central Pacific
description: Its pale yellowish body is overlaid with a fine brown network and tiny white and blue dots. Usually found in pairs resting on sand or rubble beside coral heads.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: A long, flattened green pipefish of seagrass beds and drifting weed, with a prehensile tail like a seahorse and no tail fin. It hangs among the blades, perfectly camouflaged, picking off small crustaceans.

region: Southern & south-western Australia
description: Covered in leaf-like skin lobes, it drifts like a piece of kelp, propelled by almost invisible fins. The male carries around 250 eggs embedded in a spongy brood patch under his tail; it is fully protected and kept only by public aquaria.

region: Southern Australia & Tasmania
description: Reddish with yellow spots and violet-blue bars on the chest, it drifts over kelp and seagrass on temperate rocky reefs. The male carries the eggs on a brood patch under his tail for about a month.

region: Western Pacific; invasive in the western Atlantic & Caribbean
description: Uses its fan-like pectoral fins to corner small fish and shrimp before a lightning-fast strike, while long venomous dorsal spines deter predators. Released into the western Atlantic around the 1980s–90s, it is now one of the most damaging invasive fishes on Caribbean reefs.

region: Red Sea & Indian Ocean; invasive in the eastern Mediterranean
description: The Indian Ocean twin of the red lionfish, separated mainly by counts of fin rays rather than color. Since about 2012 it has spread rapidly through the eastern Mediterranean after entering via the Suez Canal.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Society Islands
description: Dark red-brown with thin white bars and long white pectoral rays almost free of membrane; two white horizontal lines on the tail base identify it. It hides in crevices by day and hunts crabs and shrimps at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Marquesas & Japan
description: Broad reddish bars on a pale body and dark spots on the pectoral membranes set it apart, along with banded 'antennae' above the eyes. It shelters under ledges by day and hunts crustaceans at night.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Persian Gulf to Australia
description: A lionfish of muddy and sandy coastal bottoms rather than coral reefs, recognised by its plain, unspotted tail fin. Like other Pterois it herds small fish with outspread pectorals before striking.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to New Guinea
description: A small lionfish of deeper reef slopes and soft bottoms, similar to the spotfin lionfish but with more numerous, closely spaced bars and densely spotted pectoral membranes. One of the better-suited Pterois for moderate-sized tanks.

region: Hawaiian Islands (endemic)
description: Endemic to Hawaii, it hides in caves and under ledges by day and emerges at night to hunt shrimps and crabs. Broad alternating dark and pale bars cover the body, and it is only rarely exported.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: A dwarf lionfish whose broad, banded pectoral fans stay joined by membrane all the way to the ray tips. It often hunts in small groups at dusk and is hardier and smaller than the Pterois species.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: The smallest common lionfish, often found resting on rubble, seagrass or sponges with its banded, fan-like pectorals spread. Color varies from mottled brown and red to bright yellow.

region: Indo-Pacific — Mauritius to the Society Islands
description: Named for the long, whisker-like tentacles on its upper lip, this secretive dwarf lionfish has two dark eyespots on its soft dorsal fin. It hides deep in reef crevices by day and hunts small crustaceans at night.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: A drab, olive-brown dwarf lionfish endemic to Hawaii, usually sitting quietly in holes and on rubble in shallow water. It lacks the long filaments of its relatives and relies on camouflage.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea to Indonesia & Taiwan
description: A master of camouflage with a fringe of skin tassels along the chin, it lies motionless on coral, mottled like encrusting algae, until prey comes within range. Its dorsal spines carry a painful venom.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & French Polynesia
description: A humpbacked scorpionfish that mimics a lump of rubble; when disturbed it flashes the brilliant orange, yellow and black inner surfaces of its pectoral fins as a warning. It is often mistaken for the more dangerous stonefish.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Japan & New Caledonia
description: Covered in leafy skin flaps and ringed spots, it rocks gently like drifting algae and 'walks' on its pectoral and pelvic fins. It feeds almost exclusively on live fish and is a prized rarity in the trade.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Mauritius to Japan & Australia
description: Smoother than the weedy scorpionfish, with a few paddle-shaped flaps and vivid, nearly uniform pink, purple, yellow or red coloring. It sways beside algae and sponges on sandy slopes and eats only live fish.

region: Western Pacific — New Guinea, Queensland & New Caledonia
description: An intricate maze of dark lines over yellow-green or purple mimics the feather stars (crinoids) it lives among on Coral Sea reefs. One of the rarest and most expensive fishes in the aquarium trade.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Galápagos
description: Extremely compressed and leaf-like, it rocks from side to side to imitate drifting debris and regularly sheds its outer skin. Colors range from white and yellow to pink, red, brown and black.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to French Polynesia
description: The most venomous fish known: its dorsal spines inject a toxin that can kill a person. It lies half-buried and encrusted like a rock, engulfing passing fish in a fraction of a second.

region: Western Pacific — Thailand & the Philippines to Vanuatu
description: Walks across sand and mud on free, finger-like pectoral rays and buries itself up to the eyes to ambush prey. When threatened it spreads its pectorals to reveal brilliant orange, yellow and black warning colors.

region: Western Pacific — Andaman Sea to Japan & Fiji
description: Its tall dorsal fin begins right over the eyes like a cockatoo's crest; it rocks back and forth on sandy bottoms imitating a dead leaf. The dorsal spines are venomous.

region: Indo-Pacific — Mauritius to the Society Islands
description: Its skin is covered in wart-like bumps and patches of white, orange and red that mimic encrusting sponges. It twitches a fleshy lure on its first dorsal spine and can swallow fish almost its own size.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to Panama
description: The largest frogfish, found in solid yellow, orange, red, brown or black to match the sponge it sits beside, and able to change color over a few weeks on a new background. A voracious predator that needs a large tank and no smaller tankmates.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Society Islands
description: Extremely variable—black, yellow, orange, red or pink—often with a few dark, ringed spots that mimic sponge pores. The female releases her eggs in a buoyant gelatinous raft.

region: Circumtropical — Atlantic, Indian Ocean & western Pacific
description: Named for its dark wavy streaks; some individuals are covered in hair-like skin filaments that imitate algae. Its lure looks like a cluster of wriggling worms, and it often hunts on open sand and rubble.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Fiji
description: Covered in fine skin spinules that give it a shaggy look, with dark streaks radiating from the eye and a large pom-pom-shaped lure. Typically found on sand and rubble beside sponges.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: The common frogfish of Caribbean reefs, with a long, slender lure and dark ocellated spots on the body and fins. It shifts color over a couple of weeks to match nearby sponges and algae.

region: Circumtropical — floating Sargassum in the Atlantic, Indian & Pacific Oceans
description: Spends its life in rafts of floating Sargassum weed, clambering through it with grasping pectoral fins and camouflaged by fleshy tabs and mottled yellow-brown colors. A voracious predator that readily eats its own kind.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Line Islands
description: One of the most colorful groupers, orange-red peppered with tiny electric-blue spots. It lives on clear, coral-rich reef slopes and swallows any fish or shrimp that fits in its mouth.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to French Polynesia
description: Dark brown covered in small, black-edged electric-blue spots, often with several pale bars on the rear body. It lives in harems on shallow reefs and was introduced to Hawaii in the 1950s, where it is now very abundant.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: A small reddish grouper whose tail fin bears two pale diagonal bands converging toward the rear, giving it the name flagtail grouper. Small enough for large home reef tanks, where it hunts small fish and crustaceans close to shelter.

region: Western Atlantic — South Carolina to Brazil
description: A small Caribbean grouper with red-brown, bicolored or bright golden phases, always with small blue spots, two black dots on the chin and two on top of the tail base. It shelters in caves and crevices by day.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to French Polynesia
description: Orange-red with blue spots and lines and four to six dark blotches along the base of the dorsal fin. It lives in caves and often swims upside-down along cave ceilings.

region: Indo-Pacific — Comoros to the Line Islands
description: A hind of steep outer reef walls, striped with wavy blue lines on a yellow-orange body. Collected less often than other Cephalopholis and prized for its colors.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil
description: A small, shy Caribbean grouper covered in reddish-orange spots, with a row of three or four dark spots along the base of the dorsal fin. It ambushes small fish from caves and crevices.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Line Islands
description: One of the smallest groupers, reddish with crowded small spots and a pair of dark saddles on top of the tail base. It hides among branching corals and in crevices.

region: Western Pacific & eastern Indian Ocean — Japan to Australia
description: Sold as a cute polka-dotted juvenile, it grows to 70 cm and eats any fish it can swallow. Its tiny head on a steeply humped back earns it the name humpback grouper; the genus is often misspelled 'Chromileptes'.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Pitcairn Islands
description: The largest bony fish of coral reefs, exceeding 2.5 m and 400 kg; adults are mottled grey-brown while juveniles are boldly blotched black and yellow. A centerpiece of large public aquarium exhibits.

region: Atlantic — Florida to Brazil; West Africa
description: A massive, slow-growing grouper of mangroves, wrecks and reefs that can exceed 300 kg and live nearly 40 years; adults gather at traditional spawning sites. Fully protected in US waters since 1990 after severe overfishing.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Samoa
description: Covered in irregular dark brown blotches and dense small spots over a pale yellowish-brown ground, with a black saddle on the tail base. Widely farmed for food and a frequent resident of public aquarium reef exhibits.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & South Africa to Australia & Japan
description: Named for the large, potato-shaped dark blotches on its pale grey body. It is curious and often approaches divers at sites such as the Cod Hole on the Great Barrier Reef, and lives in large public aquarium exhibits.

region: Indo-Pacific — South Africa to French Polynesia
description: Pale with closely packed hexagonal brown spots forming a honeycomb, it is one of the most abundant small groupers on shallow reef flats. Like many groupers it starts life as a female and may later change to male.

region: Western Pacific — southern Japan to Australia
description: Has unusually long, fleshy pectoral fins and a pale body crowded with large dark brown spots separated by a narrow pale network. It lives on silty inshore reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Banded with five dark bars, a dark 'tuning fork' on the forehead and a black saddle on top of the tail base. Its huge winter spawning aggregations made it easy to overfish, and it is now Critically Endangered.

region: Mediterranean & eastern Atlantic; southwestern Atlantic
description: The emblematic grouper of Mediterranean rocky reefs, dark brown with pale irregular blotches and pale-edged fins. Very long-lived and slow to mature, it has rebounded in marine reserves after decades of spearfishing.

region: Western Pacific — Japan to Australia & Fiji
description: Red to orange-brown with many tiny blue spots, it is a fast-hunting reef piscivore and one of the most important food fishes of the Great Barrier Reef, where it is called coral trout. It spawns in small aggregations along the reef edge in the warmer months.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: Young fish are white with five black saddles and yellow fins, mimicking the poisonous black-saddled toby; large adults often turn dark with small blue spots. A powerful predator that can exceed a meter.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & South Africa to the Pitcairn Islands
description: A sleek grouper with a deeply crescent-shaped, yellow-edged tail and a red to purplish body sprinkled with small pink and blue spots. It hunts in open water above the reef and needs a very large tank.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: Very like the yellow-edged lyretail but with a narrow white trailing edge to the crescent tail and a dark band just inside it. It patrols outer reef slopes hunting small fishes in open water.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & South Africa to the Marquesas & Japan
description: Black with bright yellow lengthwise stripes that multiply and break into dashes as it grows. When stressed its skin releases the bitter toxin grammistin, which can kill tankmates in a closed system.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Maldives to Japan & Australia
description: Bright yellow with a black band through the eye and a broad black saddle across the middle of the body. Like other soapfishes its skin secretes a bitter, toxic mucus that deters predators.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & the Pitcairn Islands
description: Red with fine silvery-white stripes and a dark red spiny dorsal fin; it hides in crevices by day and hunts small crustaceans over sand at night with its huge eyes. Squirrelfishes communicate with audible clicks and grunts.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & the Pitcairn Islands
description: The largest squirrelfish, with a long venomous spine on each gill cover and a deep red spiny dorsal fin. It shelters under ledges by day and hunts crabs and shrimps at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marshall Islands
description: Plain red with a distinctive silvery-white patch on the tail base just behind the soft dorsal fin. It lives in small groups in caves and under ledges on lagoon and seaward reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: Striped red and silver, with white triangular tips on each dorsal spine and an elongated upper tail lobe. A common Caribbean reef fish that emerges at dusk to hunt crabs and shrimps.

region: Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil & mid-Atlantic islands
description: Silvery red with a yellowish spiny dorsal fin and a long upper tail lobe; the most widespread Atlantic squirrelfish, reaching as far as Ascension Island. It shelters in reef crevices by day.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Samoa
description: Bright red with large, dark-edged scales like a pinecone, a dark red bar on the gill cover and white leading edges to the soft fins. Groups hover in caves by day and disperse at night to feed on zooplankton.

region: Atlantic — western Atlantic & eastern Atlantic islands
description: Red with a bold black bar just behind the gill cover and white leading edges to the fins. It hangs in caves and under ledges in small groups by day and feeds on plankton in open water at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & the Pitcairn Islands
description: Silvery with lines of dark reddish spots and a large black-and-red blotch at the front of the spiny dorsal fin. It lurks among branching corals by day and feeds mainly on crabs and shrimps at night.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Maldives to Fiji & Japan
description: Juveniles are chocolate brown with large white blotches and swim with an exaggerated wriggle, thought to mimic a toxic flatworm; adults turn pale and are covered in small dark spots. They feed at night on crustaceans and worms sifted from sand.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: Adults are boldly striped black and white with yellow lips and yellow fins dotted with black, while juveniles are dark with white blotches. Often seen hovering in groups under overhangs by day, visited by cleaner wrasses.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Japan & Australia
description: Its white body is crossed by oblique black lines and its fins are yellow with black spots; juveniles are boldly blotched black and white. Adults form large daytime aggregations on reef slopes and disperse at night to feed.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia to northern Australia
description: Yellow to orange with numerous narrow, dark-edged white stripes running from head to tail. A shy species that shelters under ledges in lagoons and on coastal reefs by day.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & Bermuda to Brazil
description: Silvery with yellow stripes and two bold black bars—one slanting through the eye and one from the nape to the pectoral base. Juveniles, striped black and yellow, act as cleaners for other reef fishes.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida to Brazil
description: A deep-bodied grey grunt with dark-centered scales and a darker rear half, common around Caribbean reefs and wrecks. It feeds at night on sea urchins, crustaceans and brittle stars.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & South Carolina to Brazil
description: Bright yellow stripes, oblique below the lateral line, run over a bluish-white body. Large schools hover around coral heads by day and spread over seagrass to feed at night; grunts make their namesake sound by grinding their throat teeth.

region: Western Atlantic — South Carolina to Brazil
description: Yellow with numerous bright blue stripes and a dark soft dorsal fin and tail. Like other grunts it rests in schools over reefs by day and forages over sand and seagrass at night.

region: Western Atlantic — Chesapeake Bay to Brazil
description: Its head is marked with wavy blue and yellow lines and its body looks checkered from dark-centered scales. Pairs famously 'kiss' with open mouths, a territorial display.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to New Caledonia & Japan
description: Juveniles are white with three bold dark red bands and sometimes shelter among sea urchin spines; adults turn pinkish red as the bands fade, and can exceed a meter. It is long-lived, reaching over 30 years in the wild.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas; introduced to Hawaii
description: Bright yellow with four dark-edged blue stripes, it forms large daytime schools around coral heads and wrecks. Introduced to Hawaii in the 1950s, it has become extremely abundant there.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: Dark red with, in younger fish, two silvery-white spots along the back. A powerful predator of outer reef slopes that can live for decades; large individuals often carry ciguatera toxin.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Olive-green above and reddish below, with a small black spot below the soft dorsal fin and blue lines under the eye. A prized Caribbean food fish that forms large spawning aggregations at reef promontories.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Olive-grey with faint pale bars and bright yellow fins, with a blue line under the eye in young fish. It loiters in groups around mangroves, reefs and wrecks by day and hunts at night.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Greyish with a reddish cast and dark-edged scales, it ranges from freshwater springs and mangroves to offshore reefs. A wary, intelligent predator well known to anglers as the mangrove snapper.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Australia
description: Juveniles live in mangrove estuaries and even the lower reaches of rivers, moving offshore to reefs as they grow into large copper-red adults. Sometimes sold as a freshwater 'red snapper', but adults need full seawater.

region: Indo-West Pacific — India & Sri Lanka to the Philippines & New Guinea
description: Pale with a checkerboard of dark brown stripes and bars and a large black spot at the tail base. It lives singly or in small groups on coastal and lagoon reefs.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: Juveniles are boldly patterned black and white with long fins and swim with a wobbling motion; adults become blackish grey and school along steep reef drop-offs, feeding on plankton at night.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia to Australia & New Caledonia
description: Deep-bodied with alternating blue and yellow stripes, a yellow-ringed black spot on the tail base and long trailing dorsal and anal filaments. It cruises over sand near reefs and feeds on bottom invertebrates.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Silvery blue with a bright yellow stripe from snout to a deeply forked yellow tail. A fast, mid-water schooling snapper that often follows divers around Caribbean reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to French Polynesia
description: Juveniles drift on their sides among mangroves mimicking dead leaves, while adults are silvery discs with two dark bars that school off reef slopes. Grows quickly and needs a very large, tall tank.

region: Western Pacific — Ryukyu Islands to Australia
description: Juveniles are velvet black edged in brilliant orange with enormously tall fins, thought to mimic toxic flatworms as they swim; they are notoriously difficult to wean onto aquarium foods. Adults are silvery grey with dark bands and much shorter fins.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Papua New Guinea & Japan
description: The hardiest batfish for aquaria, silvery with dark bars and a distinctive black blotch on the lower flank in front of the anal fin. Juveniles have extremely tall dorsal and anal fins.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Silvery and disc-shaped with five or six black bars that fade with age; schools patrol wrecks and reefs. Tiny juveniles drift on their sides in shallow water looking like dead leaves or seed pods.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas & Japan
description: Deep purple-blue with red teeth and a lyre-shaped tail with long trailing lobes; vast aggregations feed on plankton above Indo-Pacific reef slopes. One of the milder triggers, it retreats headfirst into a crevice when alarmed.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Atlantic — Red Sea to Hawaii; West Africa
description: Its abstract pattern of blue and yellow lines across the face and oblique brown bands on the flank inspired the name Picasso triggerfish. It defends a territory in shallow sandy lagoons and grunts when chased.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & Easter Island
description: Hawaii's state fish, the humuhumunukunukuāpuaʻa, with a black band slanting from the eye to the belly and a black, yellow-edged wedge on the tail base. It lives on surge-swept reef flats and locks itself into holes with its dorsal spine.

region: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden & Persian Gulf
description: The Red Sea and Arabian counterpart of the Picasso triggerfish, with bright orange and blue lines on the face and rows of black spines on the tail base. Highly territorial toward tankmates.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Seychelles to Samoa & Japan
description: A small Picasso-type trigger with a large black patch on the lower belly; it lives on shallow seagrass and rubble flats. Usually less aggressive than its relatives.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: Black with large white polka dots on the lower body and a yellow, leopard-spotted saddle on the back, it is one of the most striking reef fishes. Powerful jaws crush crabs and urchins, and adults are often aggressive to all tankmates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Line Islands
description: The largest common triggerfish, notorious for charging divers who enter the cone-shaped territory above its nest during the breeding season. It crushes sea urchins, crabs and coral with powerful teeth.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: A plankton-picking trigger of outer reef slopes; males have a bright blue chin patch and yellow-margined fins, while females lack the blue. One of the few triggers usually safe with corals and peaceful fishes.

region: Pacific — Japan & Hawaii to Easter Island & Clipperton
description: Named for the fine dark lines forming a crosshatch over its scales; males have red-edged tail fins and females yellow. A zooplankton feeder of offshore islands, it is among the most expensive triggers in the trade.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & North Carolina to Brazil
description: Bluish-grey with rows of small dark spots, three black grooves on the cheek and red-edged tail lobes. A plankton feeder of deep reef walls; juveniles drift with floating Sargassum.

region: Circumtropical
description: Appears jet black but shows a greenish-blue sheen in good light, with bright pale blue lines along the bases of the dorsal and anal fins. Found throughout the tropics, often in loose groups feeding on algae and plankton above the reef.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: Dark chocolate brown with white, black-edged dorsal and anal fins and a white tail washed with pink. It grazes algae and detritus as well as small invertebrates and is one of the milder triggers.

region: Indian Ocean — Red Sea & East Africa to Indonesia
description: Black with thin white lines at the bases of the dorsal and anal fins and a white-edged tail. Usually more peaceful than other triggers, it feeds on algae, sponges and small invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Pitcairn Islands
description: Grey-brown with a white line from the mouth to the anal fin and two curved, boomerang-shaped bars behind the eye that can switch from yellow to dark brown. Less destructive than many triggers but still eats crustaceans.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: Brown with a pale belly and a white crescent along the trailing edge of the tail. It lives on shallow reef flats and seagrass and is one of the smaller triggers.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: Plain brown to grey; adult males show a yellow 'bridle' line around the chin. It lives on sand and rubble slopes, blowing jets of water to uncover buried prey.

region: Red Sea & Arabian Sea
description: Brown with a whitish tail fin; males have a bright blue throat. Common on Red Sea reefs, where it feeds on algae, sponges and small invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Society Islands
description: Juveniles are yellow-brown with blue lines, while adults become deep blue overlaid with a yellow net-like pattern. It blows jets of water into sand to expose buried prey and can be extremely aggressive when nesting.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Tuamotus
description: Tan with dark-centered scales, an orange-yellow lower face and yellow-edged fins. Breeding adults guard sand-pit nests and will attack divers that swim too close.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Line Islands & the Marquesas
description: Dark green with wavy, oblique orange lines and an orange tail; adult males lose the lines on the snout. One of the most aggressive triggers, it kills tankmates and dismantles corals and invertebrates.

region: Atlantic — western Atlantic from Canada to Brazil; eastern Atlantic islands
description: Blue, green and yellow with two bright blue stripes across the face, dark lines radiating from the eye and long filaments trailing from the tail lobes and soft dorsal. A specialist predator of long-spined sea urchins, which it flips over by blowing water to attack the unprotected underside.

region: Atlantic — Nova Scotia to Argentina; Mediterranean & eastern Atlantic
description: Olive-grey with faint dark saddles and small blue spots on the upper flank and fins, ranging from temperate to tropical waters on both sides of the Atlantic. Nesting pairs dig depressions in sand and guard their eggs.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: An obligate coral eater that feeds almost entirely on Acropora polyps, so it rarely survives without live coral. Pairs stay close together and lay their eggs among filamentous algae.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Fiji & Japan
description: A small, well-camouflaged filefish of seagrass and rubble that has become popular for eating the pest anemone Aiptasia. Males have a patch of bristles on the tail base and a larger dorsal spine.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Sri Lanka to Japan & Australia
description: Covered in branched skin tassels and marked with fine dark lengthwise lines, it hides among weed and sponges in seagrass beds and estuaries. It eats algae and small invertebrates and may pick at corals.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: Olive with an orange rear half, a vertical black bar behind the gill opening and a bright orange tail. It is shy and keeps close to reef crevices.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: Endemic to Hawaii, yellow covered in small black spots with an orange fan-shaped tail edged in black. It nibbles algae, sponges and small invertebrates and may pick at coral.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia to Samoa & Japan
description: Small and secretive, with a dark purplish head and a bright orange-red body and tail. It lives among crevices on steep reef slopes and is occasionally available to hobbyists.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Marshall Islands & Japan
description: A harmless filefish that copies the white body, four black saddles and yellow tail of the toxic black-saddled toby (Canthigaster valentini), gaining protection from predators. It can be told apart by its longer dorsal and anal fins.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida to Brazil
description: Can switch rapidly between plain brown and a pattern of large white spots, often with an orange tinge at the tail base, where males carry stiff orange spines. Usually seen in pairs grazing sponges and gorgonians.

region: Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil; eastern Atlantic islands
description: Brown with fine orange spots and pale lines, plus two conspicuous white 'tail-light' spots on top and bottom of the tail base. It grazes algae, sponges and small invertebrates on Caribbean reefs.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to Mexico
description: Grey-brown with vertical bars on the rear half, orange spines on the tail base and an orange tail. Pairs roam the reef nibbling branching coral tips, sponges and invertebrates.

region: Circumtropical
description: Long and laterally flattened, with scribbled blue lines and black spots over olive-brown and a broad, brush-like tail. It often drifts head-down among sea whips and grazes algae, hydroids and gorgonians.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Tuamotus
description: Brown with thin dark bars on the front half; males carry a brush of long spines on the tail base and females a smaller patch of dark bristles. It feeds on coral tips, sponges and algae.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: Grey, brown or yellow with scattered black spots and a dark muzzle that gives it a dog-like face. It feeds on coral tips, sponges and invertebrates and becomes very tame, begging at the glass.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to Mexico
description: Usually black with fine white spots, though some individuals are entirely golden yellow. In the wild it feeds mainly on the growing tips of branching corals.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to Panama
description: White-spotted above and striped below, with a dark, often yellow-ringed patch around the pectoral fin base; it lives in lagoons, estuaries and seagrass. Hardy and long-lived, it eats crustaceans, molluscs, urchins and coral.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to French Polynesia
description: The largest Arothron: adults are pale grey covered in small black spots, while juveniles are orange with black belly stripes. It grows too large for most home aquaria and is mainly a public-aquarium fish.

region: Indo-West Pacific — East Africa to Samoa & Japan
description: Covered in a maze of dark lines over a pale yellowish ground, with lines radiating from the eye like a map and a dark patch around the vent. A solitary species of lagoons and outer reef slopes.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Australia & Samoa
description: Pale tan with many thin dark lengthwise lines and a dark patch around the pectoral base; it lives in seagrass, mangroves and sheltered sandy areas, and juveniles enter estuaries.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Tuamotus & Japan
description: White with four black saddles, an orange-spotted face and a yellow tail, it advertises the toxins in its skin; the mimic filefish copies its pattern. Males keep harems, and females lay eggs in algae tufts.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: Orange-brown with dense blue-white spots and short blue lines along the back. Like other tobies it carries tetrodotoxin and can inflate when threatened.

region: Hawaiian Islands & Johnston Atoll
description: Endemic to Hawaii, dark brown peppered with white spots, it is one of the most common small fishes on Hawaiian reefs. It defends small territories and nibbles algae, sponges and tiny invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii
description: White with three dark brown saddles on the back, the first forming a 'crown' between the eyes, and covered in small yellow spots and blue lines. It lives on sand and rubble at the base of reefs, often deeper than other tobies.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Fiji
description: Orange-brown densely covered in small blue spots, with blue lines radiating from the eye. It is common on sheltered reefs and lagoons in the western Pacific.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: Pale with a brownish back, wavy blue and orange lines on the head and a dark, blue-ringed eyespot at the base of the dorsal fin. It lives on shallow reef flats and seagrass.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & South Carolina to Brazil
description: Brown above and white below, with blue lines radiating from the eye and dark upper and lower margins on the tail. The most common toby of Caribbean reefs and seagrass beds.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to the Galápagos
description: Olive-brown with small blue-white spots and blue lines on the head, it lives on shallow wave-swept reef flats and in surge channels. Like other tobies it is toxic to eat.

region: Indo-Pacific — eastern Indian Ocean to Hawaii & the Society Islands
description: White with a golden-brown back crossed by fine blue lines and a yellow tail. It lives on steep outer reef walls, usually below about 25 m.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to the Pitcairn Islands
description: Reddish-brown densely covered in white spots that form a honeycomb-like pattern, it is a secretive toby of caves and reef crevices.

region: Circumtropical
description: Covered in long spines that stand erect when it inflates by gulping water; tan with large dark blotches and big, appealing eyes. It crushes snails, crabs and urchins with a fused, beak-like pair of tooth plates and is most active at dusk and night.

region: Circumtropical
description: The largest porcupinefish, pale brown covered in small black spots that extend onto the fins. It hides in caves by day and hunts hard-shelled invertebrates at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: Has large dark blotches outlined in white on a pale tan body, including a dark bar below the eye. It shelters under ledges and in caves by day.

region: Western Atlantic — Maine to Brazil
description: Yellow-green with wavy dark stripes and black blotches; unlike Diodon, its short spines are fixed and permanently erect. It lives in seagrass beds and bays, eating crabs and molluscs, and can inflate when threatened.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & the Tuamotus; southeast Atlantic
description: Juveniles are bright yellow cubes with black spots; adults turn brownish-yellow with dark-edged pale spots. When stressed it releases ostracitoxin from its skin, which can kill tankmates in a closed system.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to Mexico
description: Strongly dimorphic: females are dark brown with white spots, while males have a dark, white-spotted back above blue flanks dotted with gold. It feeds on sponges, tunicates and small invertebrates.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Palau & northern Australia
description: A small, strongly dimorphic boxfish: females are brown with a pale net-like pattern, while males are more colorful, with blue on the flanks. It feeds on sponges, worms and small invertebrates on coral-rich reefs.

region: Red Sea, Gulf of Aden & Persian Gulf
description: Females are yellow with small black spots, while males develop blue flanks and a blue tail. It is restricted to the Red Sea and Arabian waters.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas
description: A yellow-green box with long, forward-pointing horns over the eyes and a very long tail fin; it hovers over sand blowing jets of water to expose buried invertebrates. Like other boxfishes it can release toxin when stressed.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii & Rapa
description: A small cowfish with horns above the eyes and a prominent spine in the middle of the back, tan with bright blue spots and lines. It lives over sand, rubble and seagrass.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Philippines
description: Its carapace is triangular in cross-section and rises to a pyramid-shaped hump topped by a single spine. It lives on sandy and seagrass bottoms and is only occasionally collected.

region: Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil; South Africa
description: Covered in bright blue scrawls and spots on a greenish-yellow body, with short horns over the eyes and a second pair of spines at the rear of the belly. It browses on seagrass, tunicates and sponges.

region: Western Atlantic — New Jersey to Brazil
description: Its carapace plates are outlined in a bold honeycomb of dark hexagons over yellow-tan, and it can shift rapidly between pale and dark color phases. Found on Caribbean reefs, often among gorgonians.

region: Western Atlantic — Massachusetts to Brazil
description: Dark with many small white spots and a pale honeycomb pattern on the flanks, lacking horns or belly spines. It blows jets of water at the sand to uncover buried invertebrates.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Papua New Guinea
description: Covered in large black spots separated by a pale yellowish honeycomb network, the balance varying from mostly white to mostly black. A large reef predator that becomes tame and takes food from tongs in captivity.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: Dark brown densely sprinkled with small white spots, with a white mouth lining that flashes when it gapes; also called the whitemouth moray. It hunts fishes and crustaceans in reef holes, mostly at night.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Marquesas & Pitcairn
description: The heaviest moray, reaching about 3 m and 30 kg, brown with black leopard spots and a black patch around the gill opening. It hunts fishes on the reef, sometimes cooperatively with roving coral groupers.

region: Western Atlantic — New Jersey to Brazil
description: Its uniform green color comes from a yellow mucus coat over dark bluish skin. A large Caribbean moray of mangroves, reefs and rocky shores that hunts fish and crustaceans at night.

region: Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil; eastern Atlantic islands
description: Dark brown peppered with small yellow spots and with a yellow tail tip; one of the smaller morays, suited to large home aquaria. It hides in reef crevices and hunts crabs and small fish.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Madagascar to the Society Islands
description: Pale greenish-yellow covered in irregular black spots, with a yellowish head. It lives in shallow lagoons and on reefs and is moderate in size for a moray.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to Panama
description: Densely mottled yellowish-brown, with a green-yellow margin to the fins and a dark spot at the gill opening. A common, bold moray of Indo-Pacific reefs.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Brazil
description: Whitish to yellow, densely covered in dark purplish-brown spots. The most common moray in the Caribbean, often seen with its head poking out of crevices on shallow reefs.

region: Southwestern Pacific — Australia & New Zealand
description: A temperate moray of rocky reefs in eastern and southern Australia and northern New Zealand, colored yellowish-brown to green with fine dark speckling. It shelters in rock crevices and tolerates cooler water than tropical morays.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to Costa Rica
description: Dark brown with an irregular pale network of lines and a yellowish-green head; known for an irritable disposition. It is mainly active at night.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to the Gulf of California
description: White with two rows of black, branching 'snowflake' blotches containing yellow spots. Its blunt, molar-like teeth crush crabs and shrimps, and it is one of the most popular aquarium morays.

region: Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil; eastern Atlantic islands
description: Black with a bright yellow chain-like network, it hunts crabs in shallow, surge-swept rocky reefs. Like other Echidna it has blunt crushing teeth.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to Hawaii & the Tuamotus
description: Ringed with 25–30 dark bands when young, fading to a mottled tan as it grows. A crab-eating moray with rounded teeth, suited to larger reef aquaria.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to French Polynesia
description: Black as a juvenile, blue with yellow fins as a male and finally yellow as a female, it lives in sand burrows with only its head out, waving leaf-like nostril flaps. Notoriously difficult to feed in captivity.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — Red Sea to Panama
description: Ringed with numerous narrow white bands on dark chocolate, it has pebble-like crushing teeth and eats only crabs, urchins and molluscs. Harmless to fishes, it is one of the best morays for aquaria.

region: Eastern Atlantic & Mediterranean — Britain to Senegal
description: Dark brown marbled with yellow and white blotches, it lives in rocky crevices from Britain to West Africa. The Romans famously kept it in seaside fish ponds.

region: Indo-Pacific — Réunion & Mauritius to Hawaii & Japan
description: Orange with dark-edged white spots, horn-like tubular nostrils and arched jaws that cannot close over its long, fang-like teeth. Highly prized and expensive, it is collected mostly in Japan and Hawaii.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Samoa
description: Extremely slender and pale with fine dark speckling, it lives in sand and rubble crevices and is a notorious escape artist through the smallest gaps.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to the Society Islands
description: Lives in colonies of hundreds, each eel rising from its own mucus-lined sand burrow to pick plankton from the current and vanishing tail-first when approached. It needs a deep, fine sand bed and gentle feeding.

region: Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil; eastern Atlantic
description: The Caribbean garden eel, brownish with fine pale speckles, forming dense colonies on sandy slopes; each fish rises from its burrow into the current to snap at plankton.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Maldives to the Philippines & Japan
description: Orange with narrow white rings, it lives in colonies on sandy slopes, often alongside the spotted garden eel, and feeds on plankton drifting past its burrow.

region: Indo-West Pacific — India to Japan & northern Australia
description: Juveniles are boldly banded black and white, fading to plain brown adults that can exceed a meter. Egg cases laid on the bottom hatch after about four months; it rests in caves by day and hunts crustaceans and fish at night.

region: Indo-West Pacific — India to Japan & Indonesia
description: Brown with dark bands and numerous small white spots, it is one of the bamboo sharks most often bred in aquaria. Captive females have produced young by parthenogenesis, without a male.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Pakistan & India to Papua New Guinea & Japan
description: Plain grey-brown as an adult, with faint bands in juveniles; a nocturnal inshore shark that feeds on crustaceans, molluscs and small fish.

region: Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea & western India
description: A slender, plain light-brown bamboo shark of the shallow, very warm Persian Gulf, where it rests among coral and rocks by day. It tolerates higher temperatures than most sharks.

region: Northern Australia & southern New Guinea — Great Barrier Reef
description: Walks across reef flats on its paddle-like fins and can survive hours of very low oxygen in tide pools at low tide. A large white-ringed black spot above each pectoral fin gives it its name.

region: Eastern Pacific — California to the Gulf of California
description: A blunt-headed, slow-moving shark with a spine in front of each dorsal fin; it crushes sea urchins and crabs with flat, molar-like rear teeth. Females wedge spiral-flanged egg cases into rock crevices.

region: Southern Australia
description: Grey with dark harness-like markings across the head and back; it returns to the same reefs each year to breed, where females screw spiral egg cases into crevices. It eats sea urchins, crabs and molluscs.

region: Northwest Pacific — Japan, Korea & China
description: Light brown with about a dozen darker bands, it lives on rocky reefs and kelp beds in Japanese and Korean waters. Females lay spiral egg cases among rocks, often at communal nesting sites.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Pakistan & India to New Guinea & the Philippines
description: A slender reef catshark patterned with dark saddles and spots and scattered white spots; one of the few sharks small enough for very large home aquaria. It lays egg cases in pairs among reef crevices.

region: Northeast Atlantic & Mediterranean
description: The most common small shark of European coasts, sandy brown with many small dark spots. Its egg cases ('mermaid's purses') are anchored to seaweed by curly tendrils and are a favourite of aquarium hatchery displays.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Solomon Islands
description: Olive-tan with electric-blue spots and a blue stripe down each side of the tail, it forages for worms, shrimps and crabs on sand flats on the rising tide and shelters under ledges. Notoriously hard to keep: many imports refuse food and fail to thrive.

region: Western Atlantic — North Carolina to Venezuela
description: Yellowish with a fine reticulated pattern of dark and pale spots that it lightens or darkens to match the sand. Small enough for very large home aquaria, it breeds readily, giving birth to live pups.

region: Eastern Pacific — California to Panama
description: A small, round-disked stingray of shallow sandy bays in California and Mexico, mottled brown with pale spots. It is a common resident of public aquarium touch pools.

region: Western Atlantic — Florida & the Bahamas to Brazil
description: Coppery and semi-translucent with a black line along the long anal-fin base, it gathers in dense schools in caves and wrecks by day and disperses at night to feed on plankton.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea to Samoa
description: Bronze to silvery with a black tip on the dorsal fin and a black edge to the anal fin; large schools fill caves and overhangs by day. It feeds on zooplankton in open water at night.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea to Fiji & Japan
description: Small and translucent golden with a silvery rear, it forms dense swirling schools in caves and over coral heads. It glows with light organs that use enzymes obtained from the bioluminescent ostracods it eats.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea to French Polynesia
description: Bright red with huge eyes and a crescent-shaped tail, it can switch rapidly to silvery or blotched red. It hovers near caves by day and hunts zooplankton and small fish at night.

region: Circumtropical
description: Red with blotchy silver bars that come and go and enormous eyes; one of the most widely distributed reef fishes, found in all tropical oceans. It shelters under ledges by day.

region: Atlantic — Nova Scotia to Argentina; eastern Atlantic
description: Bright red with very large eyes and black-spotted pelvic fins; it lives on deeper reefs and hard bottoms and gathers in loose schools at night to feed.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia to the Pitcairn Islands
description: Bluish-violet with a bright blue head and a yellow tail; pairs hover above deep rubble slopes and dive into burrows when threatened. Like other Hoplolatilus it jumps readily, so tanks need tight covers.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia
description: Its pastel lavender, yellow and blue body can flash through color changes within seconds. It lives in pairs over deep rubble and sand bottoms, retreating into a burrow when alarmed.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia to the Solomon Islands
description: Purple with a violet sheen, it lives over deep sand and rubble and dives headfirst into its burrow when alarmed. Like other Hoplolatilus it is an expert jumper.

region: Western Pacific — Philippines & Indonesia to the Solomon Islands
description: White with a single bold red stripe running from snout to tail. Pairs hover above their rubble burrows on deep reef slopes and feed on zooplankton.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Line Islands
description: Long and slender, blue above and white below with a broad black stripe toward the tail; juveniles resemble cleaner wrasses. It hovers above sand near reefs and dives into a burrow when threatened.

region: Indo-Pacific — East Africa to Hawaii
description: White with rows of orange-red blotches and a red spiny dorsal fin, it perches on its pelvic fins on sand near reefs. Smaller and better suited to aquaria than most sandperches, though it eats small shrimps.

region: Indo-Pacific — Indian Ocean to the Marshall Islands & Samoa
description: Pale with a brown lattice pattern and a row of dark spots along the lower flank; it lives in harems in which one male patrols the territories of several females on sand and rubble.

region: Western Pacific — Indonesia & the Philippines to Australia & Fiji
description: White with eight or nine dark bars, it lives on shallow sand and rubble reef flats, darting from perch to perch to snap up small crustaceans.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific — East Africa to Panama
description: Elongate with a trumpet-like snout, it hunts by hovering head-down among sea rods or by 'shadowing' larger fishes to sneak up on prey. It has brown, banded and bright yellow color phases.

region: Western Atlantic — Bermuda & Florida to Brazil
description: The Caribbean trumpetfish, drifting head-down among gorgonians to ambush small fishes and shrimps, and able to change between brown, reddish, yellow and blue-grey.

region: Indo-Pacific & eastern Pacific; invasive in the Mediterranean
description: Extremely elongate and smooth with a long whip-like filament trailing from the forked tail; it snaps up small fish with pipette-like suction. It entered the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal around 2000 and spread rapidly.

region: Atlantic — Nova Scotia to Brazil; eastern Atlantic
description: Olive-brown with a row of bright blue spots along the back and snout and a long tail filament; it hunts small fish over seagrass and reefs, often in loose groups.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Seychelles to New Caledonia & Japan
description: A wafer-thin, armored fish that swims head-down in tight synchronized schools, sheltering among sea urchin spines and branching corals. A dark stripe from snout to tail adds to its camouflage.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Persian Gulf to Japan & northern Australia
description: Very like the jointed razorfish but with a fixed, unhinged spine at the rear tip and a fainter, brownish stripe. Schools swim vertically, head-down, among seagrass and sea urchins.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea to Fiji & Japan
description: A fantastically ornamented relative of the pipefishes that hovers head-down beside feather stars and gorgonians, matching their colors. The female, not the male, broods the eggs in a pouch formed by her enlarged pelvic fins.

region: Indo-West Pacific — Red Sea to Fiji & Japan
description: Mimics a blade of seagrass or a drifting leaf in green, brown or tan, floating head-down among seagrass. The female broods the eggs between her fused pelvic fins, and the species lives only about a year.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to the Marquesas & Japan
description: A flattened, armored oddity, also called the seamoth, that 'walks' over sand on its pelvic fins and spreads wing-like pectoral fins. It sheds its entire outer skin every few days, probably to shed fouling organisms, and feeds on copepods and other tiny invertebrates.

region: Atlantic — Massachusetts to Argentina; eastern Atlantic & Mediterranean
description: It 'walks' across sand on its pelvic fins and suddenly spreads enormous, blue-spotted pectoral fins like wings to startle predators. Despite its name it cannot fly.

region: Indo-Pacific — Red Sea & East Africa to Hawaii & the Marquesas
description: Walks over sandy bottoms on its pelvic fins, probing for crustaceans, and flares huge spotted pectoral wings when alarmed. Occasionally collected for large aquaria.
